content.text: Deontic logic links its operators. O means obligatory, R means permissible, and an act is forbidden when its denial is obligatory.

content.definition: A is forbidden when O¬A: you ought not do A.
A is permissible when ¬O¬A: it is not the case that you ought not do A.
O(A) → ◇A. No one is obliged to do the impossible.

examples.title: How they relate
examples.note: Each is defined from O and ¬.

examples.title: A duty after a failed duty
lines: If you steal, you ought to return what you took.
examples.note: Rules about what to do after breaking a rule are hard to write in simple deontic logic.

question.prompt: Which formula says that A is forbidden?
question.hint: Forbidden means you ought not do it.
question.explanation: Forbidden means obligatory not to do: O¬A. ¬OA only says A is not required.
